title: Choosing a Federation Protocol: SAML, OIDC, Kerberos and LDAP

title: SCIM: Provisioning and the Identity Lifecycle
summary: SCIM 2.0 (RFC 7643 and 7644) measured against a minimal SCIM server written for the lesson in Node 22 with no framework. Discovery (ServiceProviderConfig, ResourceTypes, Schemas), create with 201 and Location, uniqueness, filters and 1-based pagination, PUT against PATCH (PUT wiped externalId and department), PatchOp with paths such as emails[type eq "work"].value, active:false against DELETE with session revocation, scimType errors (uniqueness, invalidValue, mutability, noTarget, invalidVers), ETag and If-Match, bearer rotation, groups and the group-versus-user race, JIT against SCIM, a reconciler that finds orphan accounts, server-side validation against mass assignment and privileged groups, and Entra ID, Okta and Keycloak read from their official docs only.

title: Workload Identity: Service Accounts, mTLS and SPIFFE
summary: Machine identity instead of static secrets, measured where it runs locally. A throwaway CA and mTLS with openssl, curl and a small Node server (what the server reads from the certificate SAN, refusals for a wrong CA, expiry and a missing certificate, authentication versus authorization, handshake cost), then SPIFFE/SPIRE 1.16.0 in Docker: SPIFFE IDs, X.509 and JWT SVIDs decoded and verified against the bundle, node and workload attestation with join_token and unix selectors, two workloads doing mTLS with an allow list of SPIFFE IDs, rotation at half life and the fact that revocation is the TTL. Docs only: Kubernetes projected ServiceAccount tokens, GitHub Actions OIDC federation (with the trust condition tested, including the loose repo:org/* mistake), Azure, AWS and GCP workload identity, service meshes. Ends with the anti-pattern of passing user tokens between services, rotation, audit and attribution, and a table of mechanism, what it proves, credential lifetime, who validates and the trap.

title: Privileged Access: Secrets, Vaults and Just-in-Time
summary: Privileged access and secrets, measured on HashiCorp Vault 2.2.2 in dev mode in Docker with curl, jq and the vault CLI. The problem of standing privilege and blast radius, the four parts of PAM (inventory, vault with check-out and check-in, session recording, just-in-time access), then the operation: KV v2 versions and metadata, HCL policies and three path traps, tokens with TTL, renew, expiry (403 with invalid token), revoke trees and orphans, dynamic Postgres credentials (issued, expired at the lease, revoked, and an open session that survives revocation until pg_terminate_backend is added), static role rotation and rotate-root, AppRole with response wrapping against secret zero (a second unwrap is evidence of interception), a JIT elevation approved by a second person with a 20 second token, short-lived signed SSH certificates, seal and unseal, the audit device with HMAC masked values and audit-hash, and break-glass: the Entra emergency access guidance, the MFA and Conditional Access lockout lesson, a break-glass read that raises an alert, and generate-root. Docs only: Entra PIM, Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, CyberArk, BeyondTrust, OpenBao, Vault Enterprise control groups. Ends with a comparison table of Key Vault, Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets and Vault, the PAM suite against secrets manager market, the BSL licence note, and what NIST SP 800-53 asks.
